title: Context Engineering & Guardrails
tagline: Write the constraint file that keeps an AI agent inside scope during real build work.

concept.intro: When an engineer runs an AI coding agent at Level 3 (agentic, with approval checkpoints) or Level 4 (more autonomous), the agent doesn't work off tribal knowledge — it works off whatever's written down. That written-down file is where a PM's judgment gets encoded, and increasingly, PMs are the ones best positioned to write it.

sections.heading: The autonomy spectrum
sections.body: Level 1: autocomplete — suggests the next line, a human writes everything else. Level 2: chat-assist — a human asks, the AI answers, a human still does the work. Level 3: agentic with approval — the AI plans and executes multi-step work, but checkpoints require human sign-off before anything ships. Level 4: autonomous agentic — the AI executes and ships within pre-defined bounds, with humans reviewing outcomes rather than every step. Your role changes at each level — from writing tickets, to writing the bounds the agent operates inside.

sections.heading: What goes in a guardrail file
sections.body: Project context (what this system is, in plain terms), allowed actions (what's explicitly in scope), forbidden actions (what the agent must never do, no matter how reasonable it seems in the moment), escalation rules (what triggers a stop-and-ask-a-human), and a definition of done (how anyone — human or agent — knows the work is actually finished).

sections.heading: Why this is a PM skill, not just an engineering one
sections.body: Forbidden actions and escalation rules are product judgment calls — what's an acceptable risk, what needs a human in the loop, what 'done' means for the user. An engineer can write the technical constraints; a PM is often the right person to write the product constraints. The two together are what keeps an agent safe to run at Level 3 or 4.

scenario.context: Engineering is ready to build the Returns Assistant using an AI coding agent running at Level 3 (it can write and test code across multiple files, but a human approves before anything merges).
scenario.brief: Before the engineering team starts the agent, they've asked you — the PM — to write the guardrail file that will sit alongside the code and constrain what the agent is allowed to do. This is the file the agent reads before it takes any action.

exercise.instructions: Write each section of the guardrail file. Be concrete — 'be careful' is not a constraint an agent can act on; 'never approve returns over $500 without a human sign-off' is.

prompts.label: Project context
prompts.help: What is this system, in plain terms, with no assumed prior knowledge?
prompts.placeholder: e.g. This service drafts return-approval responses for Northwind Gear Co. customers by matching requests against the current return policy document. It does not send anything directly to customers — a human agent reviews every draft.

prompts.label: Allowed actions
prompts.help: What's explicitly in scope for the agent to build or change?
prompts.placeholder: e.g. Read the policy document, draft a customer-facing response, draft an internal note citing the policy section, flag a request for escalation.

prompts.label: Forbidden actions
prompts.help: What must the agent never do, even if it seems reasonable in context?
prompts.placeholder: e.g. Never auto-send a response to a customer. Never approve a return over $500 without a human sign-off flag. Never state a policy that isn't present in the source document. Never modify the policy document itself.

prompts.label: Escalation rules
prompts.help: What situations should stop the agent and require a human decision?
prompts.placeholder: e.g. Any request tagged as a VIP account. Any return amount over $500. Any request where the policy document doesn't clearly cover the situation.

prompts.label: Definition of done
prompts.help: How would anyone — human or agent — know this work is actually finished and safe to ship?
prompts.placeholder: e.g. Every drafted response cites a specific policy section. All test cases from the historical request set produce the correct escalation flag. No test case contains a fabricated policy statement.
